catalog_quote: M. has a seven-vowel system: i, e, ɛ, a, u, o, ɔ. M. utilizes three levels of tone on the word-level, both lexically and grammatically: low (`), high (¯), and superhigh (´), of which the superhigh level is best described as phonological stress rather than tone (s. Diehl 2007). Within one segmental mora there are a few cases of high-low tone combination, as in bɔ̄̀r 'honey'. There are no syllable-initial consonant clusters. ... Tone is not used to mark case. With regard to number, the nominal system includes singulative and plural marking, utilizing multiple suffixes and sometimes tone changes ... Functioning as demonstratives is a set of toneless clitics
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Me'en (meen1242) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Diehl 2007 'The Effect of a Floating Stress Feature with Certain Toneless Morphemes in Me'en' (Payne & Reh eds., Advances in Nilo-Saharan Linguistics, Köppe, pp. 73-88), is squarely about word stress in this language but is not open anywhere found (paid Köppe PDF only, no DOI, no Google Books preview, not on archive.org; Two reviews were obtained instead: the open Piłaszewicz review in SALC 41 (fetched sources, saved) confirms pp. 73-88 and summarises the paper (toneless morphemes trigger retroactive pitch-raising; the floating stress feature is a lexical property, quoting Diehl p. 87), and a JALL 30 (2009) review (Google Books snippet only, De Gruyter blocked) says Diehl shows the ultra-high tone is the realisation of stress on a high tone. The best first-hand statement actually read remains Diehl & Will's Encyclopaedia Aethiopica 3 (2007) article, p. 908, already on file: three tone levels L/H/superhigh, 'of which the superhigh level is best described as phonological stress rather than tone (s. Diehl 2007)'; Will 1989 p. 130 is explicitly silent ('Tone and stress have not yet been sufficiently investigated'). No source gives a fixed positional stress rule; Me'en reads as a tone language with lexically/morphologically placed stress. Acquiring Diehl 2007 is high priority as the deciding source. new_statements.rule_in_words: Me'en is a tone language (Low vs High, lexical and grammatical); a third, culminative 'superhigh' pitch level is analysed not as a tone but as phonological stress (per Diehl 2007, a floating stress feature realised as extra-high pitch on a High-toned mora). The encyclopedia entry gives no positional rule for which syllable carries it, i.e. stress placement is treated as a lexical/morphological property marked in transcription, not predictable from word edges.
new_statements.exceptions: Demonstrative enclitics (-dia, -dogo, -dua, -dica) are described as toneless clitics; some number marking involves tone changes. No stress exceptions discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('three levels of tone on the word-level'); transcriptions are citation forms with tone/stress diacritics. The fuller argument (stress only realisable on a H-tone mora; floating stress with toneless morphemes) is in Diehl 2007, which could not be opened; Will 1989 p. 130 explicitly says 'Tone and stress have not yet been sufficiently investigated.'
new_statements.identity_note: Diehl & Will 2007 describe Me'en as a whole (glottocode meen1242), noting the two main dialects Tishana (Tishena) and Bodi; Diehl's SIL fieldwork underlying the tone/stress analysis is on the Tishena (western) variety. Will 1989 is based mainly on Tishena data as well.

new_statements.reading: Me'en is a tone language (L/H, lexical and grammatical) with a culminative 'superhigh' pitch level that its principal analyst (Diehl) treats as phonological stress realised on a high-toned mora; stress is thus a lexical/morphological property (Diehl 2007: a floating stress feature on certain toneless morphemes, retroactive pitch-raising, to be listed in the lexicon) and no fixed positional stress rule is stated in any source read. Coding suggestion if entered: tone language with lexically placed (non-positional) stress / 'no fixed stress'; deciding source would remain Diehl 2007 pp. 73-88 once obtained. This statement was already on file from the earlier pass; this sweep added the two reviews that corroborate it and fixed the page range.

sources.citation: Piłaszewicz, Stanisław (2007/2008). Review of Doris L. Payne & Mechthild Reh (eds.), Advances in Nilo-Saharan Linguistics (NISA 22, Köln: Köppe 2007, 294 pp.). Studies of the Department of African Languages and Cultures 41: 161-165. ISSN 0860-4649.
sources.quote: A. Diehl in „The Effect of a Floating Stress Feature with Certain Toneless Morphemes in Me'en" (pp. 73-88) tries to explain why certain toneless morphemes in Me'en (an Eastern Sudanic language spoken by about 50.000 people in the South-West of Ethiopia) trigger pitch-raising retroactively. He concludes that the phenomenon „[...] needs to be recorded in the lexicon, since it is part of the morpheme's lexical properties" (p. 87).
sources.note: Second-hand summary of Diehl 2007: a floating stress feature on certain toneless morphemes raises pitch retroactively (on the preceding mora) and is a lexical property of the morpheme. Confirms the page range 73-88.
